title: Predicting human decisions with behavioural theories and machine learning
one_line: The authors combine a behavioural decision theory with gradient-boosted trees (BEAST-GB) so that theory-derived features feed a machine-learning model that predicts human risky choice better than either approach alone.
key_claims: Hybrid approach: features generated by an established behavioural theory of decisions from description and experience are supplied to a machine-learning ensemble, which then predicts aggregate human choice rates.
The hybrid model outperforms both the pure behavioural theory and machine learning trained on raw task/problem descriptors alone.
The authors report winning/leading performance in a large choice-prediction competition setting and generalisation to held-out datasets not used for training.
Theory-based features are claimed to be the main driver of predictive gain, implying behavioural theory acts as useful inductive bias rather than being superseded by ML.
The framework is presented as a general recipe: use theory to define the feature space, use ML to capture residual regularities theory misses.
limitations: Show notes contain only the DOI, so specific effect sizes, accuracy metrics and sample sizes could not be verified from the supplied material.
Predictions are largely of aggregate choice rates across problems rather than individual-level decisions.
Performance is demonstrated within the family of monetary gamble/risky-choice paradigms; transfer to other decision domains is not established here.
Improved prediction does not by itself yield improved mechanistic explanation of the underlying cognitive process.
open_questions: Does the theory-plus-ML advantage survive on genuinely out-of-distribution decision tasks collected by other labs?
How much of the gain remains if the behavioural theory's features are replaced by a large, atheoretical feature set of comparable size?
Can the fitted model be inverted to generate new, testable behavioural hypotheses rather than only predictions?
